title: 001IC - A Guidelines Approach to Complex Urethral Stricture Disease
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Advances in the Evaluation and Management of Urethral Stricture Disease
The evaluation and management of urethral stricture disease continues to evolve with advances in our understanding of stricture pathophysiology, innovations in surgical technique, and novel drug delivery strategies. In this course, members of the AUA Guideline Panel will present evidence-based updates on the diagnosis and treatment of urethral stricture, building on the 2017 AUA Guideline and the 2023 update.
This course will incorporate the most recent literature and broadened scope of the guidelines to include female urethral stricture disease. Through a case-based format, participants will explore clinical decision-making using imaging, surgical videos, and interactive audience response systems to facilitate active learning.
Expanded topics for in-depth discussion include:
- Diagnosis and treatment of female urethral stricture, including graft and flap-based reconstructive techniques
- Evidence supporting adjunctive intralesional drug delivery following endoscopic treatment
- Counseling patients on quality-of-life outcomes and expectations using shared decision-making frameworks
- Advances in bulbar urethroplasty, including non-transecting techniques
-Advanced reconstructive techniques for fossa navicularis and penile urethral strictures
- Management of bladder neck contractures, including endoscopic and robotic bladder neck reconstruction
By the end of this course, participants will have enhanced their knowledge of urethral stricture disease and be better equipped to lead comprehensive, patient-centered discussions regarding treatment options and expected outcomes.

Learning Objective 1: Describe the complete evaluation of a new stricture patient, male or female, interpret the relevant diagnostic tests

Learning Objective 2: Identify situations in which immediate dilation of a stricture or suprapubic cystotomy is indicated prior to initiation of a formal workup and treatment.

Learning Objective 3: Determine appropriateness of adjunctive local drug delivery technologies after endoscopic treatment of bulbar urethral stricture.

Learning Objective 4: Evaluate the relative risks and benefits of endoscopic versus robotic versus open reconstruction of vesicourethral anastomotic stricture after radical prostatectomy.

Learning Objective 5: Identify various reconstructive techniques for complex urethral stricture and bladder neck contracture.

title: 002IC - Contemporary Pharmacotherapy for Overactive Bladder 2026: Monotherapy and Combined Pharmacotherapy to Optimize Treatment

Course Description: Much has been written and debated about drug treatment of overactive bladder (OAB) over the past two decades. Nevertheless, the field continues to evolve. OAB pharmacotherapy remains an area of active investigation, and innovation. The updated AUA/SUFU guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of overactive bladder (non-neurogenic) in adults as well as the recently published proceedings of the 8th International Consultation on Incontinence has maintained considerable interest in this area amongst researchers and practitioners. This course will outline the new AUA/SUFU Guideline, describe the physiological and pharmacological underpinnings of modern drug treatment of overactive bladder, review currently available agents, and discuss agents in development.

Learning Objective 1: Define the similarities and differences between the various oral pharmacotherapies for overactive bladder (OAB)

Learning Objective 2: Review the principles of physiology and pharmacotherapy for currently available agents including the antimuscarinics and beta-3 agonists

Learning Objective 3: Review the salient features as well as changes in the updated AUA/SUFU guideline on OAB

Learning Objective 4: Analyze the clinical (and theoretical) advantages and limitations of currently available agents

Learning Objective 5: Discuss potential future pharmacological pathways and therapies for OAB

title: 003IC - Vaginal Surgery for the Urologist: Urinary Incontinence, Fistulae, and Pelvic Organ Prolapse
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Vaginal Surgery for the Urologist is a practical surgical techniques course which will cover the major cases involving vaginal reconstructive surgery. In 2026 the course will focus on vaginal surgery for the treatment of urinary incontinence (including stress incontinence and fistulae) and pelvic organ prolapse. The course will cover the most common and complex vaginal procedures performed by urologists featuring five experienced vaginal surgeons, from three “urology generations”. The diverse faculty will bring unique surgical insights to the course. The course will not include didactic sessions, but rather teaching by videos, faculty panel, and audience discussions. The course will be heavily weighted towards practical aspects and tips and tricks of vaginal surgery, specifically geared toward the practicing urologist. While we will incorporate evidence-based outcomes in all appropriate areas, the focus will be on surgical approach and technique. In 2026 we will focus on surgery for incontinence including stress urinary incontinence, vesicovaginal fistula and urethrovaginal fistula. We will also focus on pelvic organ prolapse for all three compartments. We will address the question: why and when to consider surgery via a vaginal approach. We will discuss general principles of vaginal surgery (incisions, dissection and exposure). The course will be technique focused and will utilize videos from actual cases to show different surgical techniques with comments from each of the faculty. We will also discuss alternative techniques including those proposed by faculty as well as course participants as well as complications from surgery. There will be extensive audience lead discussions among faculty and participants. Participants are also encouraged to bring challenging cases to the faculty for open discussion.

title: 005IC - Bladder Cancer in the Office from Indolent to Aggressive: A Practical Guideline-based Approach
htmlDescription:
Course Description: There are several emerging and newly FDA-approved intravesical therapies for early-stage bladder cancer. With the proliferation of options (e.g. nadofaragene, nogapendekin, gemcitabine/docetaxel, pembrolizumab), it is critical to understand 1) indications for these agents, 2) timing and sequencing of administration, and 3) management of common side effects. We will discuss how to bring these treatments to your clinic and set up your team for efficiency and success.
Many urologists co-manage patients with advanced bladder cancer with their medical oncology, radiation oncology, and palliative care colleagues. New systemic therapies have emerged (e.g. enfortumab vedotin, pembrolizumab, erdafitinib) and urology providers need to be aware of the changing landscape of advanced disease. We will dive into the indications and common side effects of these therapies to provide urologists and advanced practice providers with the skills and knowledge to address potential problems.
This course will be interactive, guideline-based (AUA and NCCN), and include cases from the faculty’s clinical practices.

Learning Objective 2: Define the FDA indications and describe the efficacy of various intravesical therapies.

Learning Objective 3: Identify the proper sequence of intravesical therapies for non-muscle invasive bladder cancer.

Learning Objective 4: Describe the logistics and safe handling of novel intravesical therapies.

Learning Objective 5: Identify and manage the side effects and toxicities of novel intravesical therapies.

title: 007IC - Optimizing Geriatric Urologic Care: A High-Yield Primer on Risk Stratification, Shared-Decision-Making, and the Perioperative Care of Older Adults
htmlDescription:
Course Description: As a specialty, urology has consistently been ranked as one with the largest volume of care for older adults (> 65 years of age) and we are projected to face a significant increase in the number of older adults we will care for in the coming years. An evidence-based approach to risk stratification and perioperative management and a familiarity with key principles of geriatric medicine are crucial to caring for our older and medically complex patients. This course will provide a high-yield review of commonly encountered problems in older adults. We will detail the fundamental tenets of geriatric care that are immediately adoptable to learners’ clinical practice. Learners will gain the ability to quickly assess frailty, comorbidity, nutrition, mental health, cognition, and resilience and we will provide a “geriatric care toolbox” for participants including all instruments and tools discussed for easy transfer to clinical care pathways. We will highlight effective strategies to elicit goals of care and provide an efficient framework to guide development of priority-aligned treatment plans for older and medically complex patients. We will also address critical ethical and relevant social issues of importance for the care of older patients, including issues around consent, capacity, and complex decision-making. Finally, we will highlight how these tools can guide not only selection for pretreatment interventions, but also perioperative management with the goal of enhancing recovery and mitigating operative risk through personalized and pragmatic prehabilitation strategies. This course will benefit trainees, physicians, nurses, and advanced practice providers.

Learning Objective 1: Describe common challenges in the evaluation and management of complex geriatric patients regarding multimorbidity management and urologic care needs

Learning Objective 2: Outline the critical the components of a comprehensive personalized preoperative clinical assessment for older and medically complex patients to guide assessments of candidacy for therapy, predict postoperative complications, and estimate recovery

Learning Objective 3: Define key geriatric constructs that inform risk assessment including frailty, functional status, and resilience, and empower the learner to efficiently evaluate these domains to guide clinical recommendations in routine practice.

Learning Objective 4: Augment providers’ shared decision-making skills, discussing the central tenets of shared decision-making, providing learners with an effective framework to elicit goals of care and provide older patients with a bespoke treatment approach aligned with individual priorities. In doing so, we will define and discuss the intricacies and ethics around complex decision-making highlighting concepts relevant to older adults including advanced care planning, capacity, surrogate decision-making and conservatorships.

Learning Objective 5: Provide a pragmatic approach to risk-adapted prehabilitation and perioperative optimization based on a patient’s unique geriatric-assessment based vulnerability profile

title: 020IC - Navigating Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM): Path to Patient SatisfactioN
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is a term that describes the spectrum of symptoms and signs caused by hypoestrogenic changes in urogenital tissues typically occurring during menopause. Symptoms of GSM may include vulvovaginal dryness, burning, and irritation; sexual symptoms of lack of lubrication, discomfort or pain, or impaired function; and urinary symptoms of urgency, dysuria, or recurrent urinary tract infections. An unfortunate barrier to treatment is that women believe symptoms of GSM are a normal consequence of aging that they must accept. As a result, women rarely discuss symptoms with their healthcare provider and providers do not consistently ask about symptoms.
This course reviews the recently released AUA GSM guidelines and synthesizes the totality of evidence available on the benefits and harms of screening, diagnosis and treatment of GSM will inform decision-making for healthcare professionals, clinicians, patients, and caregivers.

htmlDescription:
Course Description: This is an ongoing course on advanced prostate cancer at the annual AUA since 2012 and the changes over the last decade continue to be breathtaking! Advanced prostate cancer made national news headlines in 2025 as the former President of the United States was diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer continuing to make this a timely and important topic. In this case-based program featuring urologists and a World-Renowned GU Medical Oncologist, we will update the audience on the management of high-risk biochemical recurrence, non-metastatic CRPC (M0 CRPC), new M1 Hormone-sensitive disease, and metastatic hormone refractory prostate cancer (mCRPC). We will discuss that many patients are initially managed by urologists and their APP practice colleagues and steps to ensure a smooth team approach to complex care.
Using a case based and multi-disciplinary format, we will continue to push the boundaries of knowledge to urologists and their teams in covering this new toolbox of novel therapies. In addition, we will cover the latest advance in molecular genetic profiling, PARP
inhibitors, and "Triple" therapy for HS M1 disease. The course faculty will be an academic urologist, a LUGPA Private Practice Urologist, an Academic Medical Oncologist

title: 011IC - Practical Implementation of Advanced Minimally Invasive Therapies for Overactive Bladder: A Case-based Course
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a common condition that affects millions of people worldwide. It presents a tremendous quality of life issue, preventing people from living their fullest lives. The fact is, there are many successful options for us to offer our patients.

In this UPDATED course (borne from a course that has been offered for several years), learners will be presented with a case-based discussion incorporating the 2024 AUA/SUFU OAB guidelines regarding how to navigate and integrate available minimally invasive therapies (previously referred to as 3rd line therapies) for patients for whom non-invasive therapies such as dietary modification, urgency suppression techniques, and physical therapy, and pharmacotherapies are not successful.

Attendees will be instructed on optimal technique for application of minimally invasive therapies, such as optimal lead placement, troubleshooting neurostimulators, technique and equipment for onabotulinumtoxinA injection, and placement of tibial nerve stimulation. Attendees will also learn how to optimize integration of minimally invasive therapies into their practice flow with minimal disruption, presentation (scripting) techniques to impart important information to patients with user-friendly comprehensible language and analogies to help the patients receive the counseling, pros and cons of each of the minimally invasive therapies, technical tips on optimal delivery of the four FDA-approved minimally invasive therapies (sacral neuromodulation, tibial nerve stimulation (percutaneous or implanted), and onabotulinumtoxinA injection) and how to select which therapies are the best fit for a given patient. The format, again, will be case based, but also conversational and interactive, with the use of the audience response system and encouragement for live real-time audience discussion.

Learning Objective 1: Discuss the treatment of OAB in the context of the updated 2024 AUA/SUFU OAB Guidelines.

Learning Objective 2: Discuss the minimally-invasive therapies available to treat OAB refractory to conservative techniques.

Learning Objective 3: Effectively provide counseling regarding advanced treatment techniques with "friendly, nonthreatening" language that does not intimidate the patients.

Learning Objective 4: Consider helpful techniques to optimize lead placement (both for percutaneous nerve evaluation (PNE) and full or staged implantation in the operating room) for sacral neuromodulation and be comfortable with troubleshooting the device.

Learning Objective 5: Incorporate caveats that are important in the delivery of onabotulinumtoxinA injections in the bladder for treatment of OAB.

Learning Objective 6: Incorporate peripheral nerve stimulation options, including the traditional and newer techniques that will be discussed in detail, into their practice as they see fit.

Learning Objective 7: Be familiar with the new implantable tibial nerve stimulation devices and techniques.

Learning Objective 8: Be aware of and familiar with new options on the horizon for treatment of refractory overactive bladder.

title: 012IC - Dust or Bust: A Guide to Modern Day Laser Lithotripsy Strategies for Ureteroscopy
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Modern-day lasers are able tocan fragment stones using settings that incorporate a variety of selection parameters: frequency, pulse energy, pulse duration and pulse modulation. The options of lasers have increased from low low-power to high high-power holmium systems and now the super pulse thulium fiber laser. This course teaches the practicing urologist the rationale behind the selection of which laser and why for laser lithotripsy, and the various parameters to choose for safe and efficient ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy. Various strategies for a dusting and fragmentation approach to endoscopic laser stone surgery will be taught via video-based case discussion. Participants will be able to identify patients with upper urinary tract stones suitable for fragmentation or dusting techniques. They will understand the differences between the holmium vs. thulium laser wavelength and the advantages to each system. The evidence based on stone clearance and quality of life after laser lithotripsy will be discussed, including literature on recurrence rates and retreatment. Standardized algorithms, along with tips and tricks, will open the door for advanced laser strategies in this rapidly evolving field.

title: 013IC - 10 Must-Knows for Pelvic Pain - To Always Do and Never Miss
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Five experts will impart what they want learners to ALWAYS CATCH and NEVER MISS in the approach to pelvic pain. These 10 must-knows will be presented in clear, highly visual image and video-rich case vignettes. The course is ideal for advanced practice providers and MDs to attend together for practice building, or for trainees to optimize efficiency in approaching pelvic pain. This year's offering will build on our 2025 course, "Surgical Interventions for Pelvic Pain and What to Do With Everyone Else", carrying many of the same themes (differential diagnosis, multispecialty care, surgical vs. medical management). The AUA 2026 course will bring diagnostic, medical and surgical pearls alive through real-life case examples: 1)- When should a person with interstitial cystitis be offered cystectomy, and show me the technique. - 2) Hormonal therapy for vulvar pain is that simple? And there's a guideline to protect me? - 3) Is bladder neck obstruction all that's causing 10/10 pain? And it's a surgical fix? 4)- I don't need to do an orchiectomy to address this situation? 5)- My patient's pelvic pain is undiagnosed multiple sclerosis? 6)- Neuromodulation can fix that? 7)- I missed endometriosis? 8)- Surgery should be the last resort on this type of patient? How do I identify them? The approach will engage the learner through relatable scenarios, showing them how much they already know, and filling in the gaps that are holding them back.

Learning Objective 2: Manage five foundational causes of pelvic pain we know you can master.

Course Description: This course will present an in-depth approach to the latest clinical developments in the diagnosis and medical/surgical treatment of the infertile male. title: 015IC - Essential in Prostate Cancer Focal Therapy: From the Classroom to the Operating Room Utilizing Novel Techniques and High Quality Clinical Evidence
htmlDescription:
Course Description: The course is designed to provide urologists (attendings, fellows, residents) and advanced practice providers a foundational knowledge of the evidence supporting focal therapy for localized prostate cancer. The instructors will critically review retrospective data and prospective trials focusing on patient populations and selection, oncological outcomes measured, and patient-reported quality of life. The information will be provided in a case-based format with a focus on patient-physician communication skills training to describe the risks/benefits of focal therapy. appropriately set patient expectations and boost the appropriateness of essential follow-up including post treatment biopsies using behavioral psychology techniques used by negotiation experts. The goal is to provide adequate tools to expand physician-patient trust and improve shared-decision making. Further, we will implement a novel flipped classroom structure to teach basics of quality-of-life assessment adapted to focal therapy and provide novel methods to assess these outcomes in all settings: academic practice and private practice. A new dimension for the 2025/2026 course application is incorporating videos of techniques with each ablation technology linked with the case presentation and learning objectives. Our goal remains to provide an educational course agnostic of focal therapy technology.

Learning Objective 1:Master a comprehensive fund of knowledge about retrospective studies and prospective clinical trials in focal therapy from 2010 to present. Learning objective number 1 will be focused on presenting and comparing patient populations across studies. These concepts will be taught using case-based discussion which will translate into a foundational knowledge of appropriate selection criteria for focal therapy. The discussion will be nuanced to describe patient selection based on diagnostic modality: transrectal or transperineal prostate biopsy and MR-targeted or systematic-based biopsy only to generalize the findings to all populations of participants including academic and private-based office practice and rural or urban settings. A new edition for the 2025/2026 course is providing the didactic heavy materials on trials/clinical data/technology description in the pre-course material to maximize learning during the course at the AUA.

Learning Objective 2: Focus on oncologic based outcomes. The participants will be able to describe endpoints in studies and an emphases will be made to compare across studies. The goal of this objective is to provide participants a fund of knowledge to understand appropriate follow-up regimens and discuss risks and benefits with patients. In this objective, the instructors will provide a systematic communication tool for physicians and APPs to engage in shared decision making and obtain informed medical consent for focal therapy agnostic of treatment modality. The treatment modalities discussed will be limited to devices approved by the FDA for prostate tissue ablation or cancer-indication. In addition, a focus will be on documentation of patient-physician discussions and essential elements of goals of care for informed medical consent.

Learning Objective 3: Review quality of life data presented in retrospective studies and prospective clinical trials in focal therapy. An emphases in this objective will be on comparative data and a detailed discussion will include patient-reported quality of life data from radiation therapy trials and radical prostatectomy trials. This session will be highlighted by case based discussions of difficult patients and managing expectations. Specifically, the authors will go into detail about pitfalls in discussing sexual function outcomes including erectile function vs overall sexual satisfaction. The instructors will engage the audience and challenge them to provide responses to difficult patient situations including ejaculatory dissatisfaction, infertility, pelvic pain, and psychological erectile dysfunction.

Learning Objective 4: Approach each patient's cancer with an agnostic approach to device and energy source. Instead of focusing on a one-size fits all approach, the course faculty will describe their choice of device and energy source based on key characteristics for every case. The faculty has been chosen to represent experience with all currently available focal therapy devices and energy sources. No single device will be emphasized but the advantages of using a particular device for a specific case will be highlighted. The audience will be polled on current experience with devices and energy sources to guide the case-based discussion. Importantly, a session will be dedicated to providing a mission statement and guiding principles for starting a successful clinical focal therapy program. Attendees will be able to start and sustain a focal therapy program (reimbursement, hospital stakeholders) and they will be challenged to reflect on ethical issues providing a novel treatment modality.

Learning Objective 5: Confidently approach common and serious complications after focal therapy. The instructors will highlight cases with high-quality pictures and videos describing methods to identify complications (i.e. urethral strictures, rectal fistula) and techniques to overcome these setbacks. The learning objective will entail effective communication pre-treatment regarding complications and safe practices to prevent complications after focal therapy. The emphasis of the clinical cases will be to challenge the participants to approach each case thoughtfully and provide access to the experts after the course (email) to provide mentorship and guidance in these difficult cases.

title: 018IC - Complications of Robotic Urological Surgery: Prevention, Recognition, and Management
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Robotic surgery in urology is growing rapidly. It is often perceived as “glamorous” and an “in thing.” Many surgeons start performing robotic surgeries simply because their hospital acquired a new robot, without being fully aware of the potential harm that can occur without proper training, awareness and exposure. It is estimated that over 500,000 robotic procedures have been performed to date, and growth in robotic procedures is expected to be about 10% per year. In parallel, the emergence of single-port robotic surgery has introduced an additional layer of complexity. While this technology offers benefits such as reduced invasiveness and improved cosmetic outcomes, it also presents distinct technical challenges, ergonomic constraints and an increased risk of complications when performed by inexperienced surgeons. At the same time, there have been several reports and lawsuits pertaining to major complications from robotic surgery. It is imperative that urologists embarking on a career involving robotic surgeries be aware of the potential complications, as well as how to prevent and manage them. We all know that there is significant underreporting of complications, and most trainees coming into practice have little knowledge and experience with dealing with robotic complications. Existing practitioners embark on robotic surgeries without being aware of what harm is possible with little knowledge, few skills and limited experience. This proposed course seeks to address this important gap between perception and reality.

Learning Objective 2: Prevent and manage robotic surgical complications by viewing a vivid video demonstration of a catastrophe,
providing awareness and prevention of such an occurrence in the course attendee’s practice. Many
complications occur due to misidentification of the anatomy, surgeon disorientation and “biting off more
than one can chew.” These scenarios will be highlighted extensively during the course.

Learning Objective 3: Identify robotic complications. Be aware of the possible harm in robotic surgeries with little knowledge, few
skills and limited experience. The proposed course seeks to address this critical gap between perception and reality.

title: 019IC - Current Concepts and Controversies in Male Hormone Replacement Therapy
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Testosterone (T) is the primary androgenic hormone responsible for the development of male sex organs and the maintenance of secondary sex characteristics. The diagnosis of male hypogonadism requires both a specific serum T level (≤300 mg/dL) and corresponding clinical symptoms. This course explores numerous methods of T replacement therapy aimed at restoring physiological androgen levels and alleviating symptoms. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve gonadotropin administration or T supplementation. Despite existing guidelines from multiple medical societies, several aspects of testosterone deficiency (TD) remain controversial. Structured to address these debates, this case-based course provides guidance on evaluating and managing TD. Faculty will integrate established guidelines with clinical expertise to deliver a comprehensive perspective. Participants will examine the clinical implications of free versus total T in TD assessment, the diverse factors influencing T levels, and key concerns such as polycythemia, gynecomastia, bone density, and hyperprolactinemia. The course will also critically analyze available TD assessment questionnaires and explore the impact of T therapy on male fertility, cardiovascular health, and prostate-related conditions, including prostate cancer. In addition to these foundational topics, the course covers emerging concepts in T therapy. This includes the use of T in transgender patients, its potential role as an endothelial modulator, and the concept of bipolar T therapy for advanced prostate cancer. Participants will also explore T therapy as a performance enhancer, gaining insight into its evolving applications. Designed for clinicians involved in TD management, this course provides essential knowledge for optimizing patient care amid ongoing debates in the field.

Learning Objective 1: Recognize the clinical presentation and standard diagnostic methods used for identifying male hypogonadism/testosterone deficiency.

Learning Objective 2: Fully comprehend the cardiovascular implications of testosterone replacement therapy (including recent Traverse study results) and the relationship of the metabolic syndrome to testosterone deficiency.

Learning Objective 3: Identify the scientific basis and benefits for androgen replacement therapy and its potential risks/consequences (e.g., polycythemia).

Learning Objective 4: Appraise the controversy regarding testosterone replacement therapy and prostate cancer/benign prostatic hyperplasia/male fertility.

Learning Objective 5: Gain knowledge on natural ways to improve testosterone values.

Learning Objective 6: Devise a cost-effective treatment and follow-up algorithm for the hypogonadal male.

title: 022IC - Advancing Patient Care in IC/BPS: Insights From Research and Clinical Practice
htmlDescription:
Course Description: This course on interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome is designed for the urologist, gynecologist, and advanced practice providers who see these patients and are responsible for their medical care. It is designed to focus on what we know, what we have learned from recent research efforts, how we can best use our knowledge in the care of these patients, and what may be coming in the future. We will discuss definition, nomenclature, epidemiology, and possible etiology, and review the recently updated AUA Guideline which provides a working framework from which to practice. We will discuss emerging data about the diagnosis and management of patients with Hunner lesion disease. We will also discuss the potential role of the urinary microbiome and molecular diagnostic techniques in the etiology and evaluation of IC/BPS. Finally, we will review the major findings of the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases Multidisciplinary Approach to the study of Chronic Pelvic Pain (MAPP) Research Network, which is completing over a decade of intensive research on this syndrome. How might this research inform and translate into the clinical arena and help our patients now and in the future? The session will conclude with questions and comments from the attendees.

title: 024IC - Practical AI for Practicing Urologists
htmlDescription:
Course Description: At AUA2024 and AUA2025, we introduced “Practical AI for Practicing Urologists,” the first AI-focused course at an AUA meeting, translating machine learning tools into clinical practice. Attendance grew from 338 registrants in 2024 to over 500 in 2025—so many that the room was filled to capacity and latecomers had to stand or leave. This enthusiasm—even in a less-than-ideal time slot—underscores urologists’ hunger for practical AI guidance as the field advances rapidly.
Building on this momentum, we propose an enhanced generative AI (GAI) course for AUA2026. By diving deeper into the latest GAI breakthroughs and their sophisticated applications, we aim to equip urologists with actionable skills to improve patient care, streamline workflows, and boost outcomes.

The relentless expansion of medical knowledge, combined with EMR‐related burdens and regulatory demands, has contributed to burnout in 54% of U.S. urologists—the highest rate across specialties (Medscape, 2021). Burnout increases diagnostic errors, jeopardizing patient safety. AI‐driven automation can alleviate these pressures by minimizing repetitive tasks and cognitive load.
Generative AI is already reshaping medicine: ChatGPT reached over 100 million users within three months of its December 2022 launch (Bienasz, 2023). Healthcare AI research has exploded—over 1,279 prostate cancer AI/ML publications in the past decade, growing 79% annually (Cacciamani et al., unpublished). The FDA has cleared 884 AI/ML–enabled devices since 1995, 98% after 2014 and 30% since 2023 (FDA, 05/19/2024). Venture funding totaled $1.1 billion in 2023–24. Given these trends, deep AI literacy is essential for urologists.
Our AUA2026 course will feature leading experts from Google, Microsoft, and academia, focusing on three pillars:
1- AI Fundamentals
Demystify AI concepts with intuitive, math‐free explanations.
Address capabilities, limitations, ethics, and risk mitigation.
2- Clinical Applications
Demonstrate AI tools for automated history taking, note generation, and workflow optimization.
Highlight AI‐driven imaging analysis to reduce diagnostic errors and enhance care.
Share real‐world case studies showing time savings and revenue impact.
3- Research Integration
Introduce AI tools for literature review, data analysis, and manuscript drafting.
Review ethical guidelines for AI/ML and ChatGPT in research (Lee et al., 2023; Cacciamani et al., 2023).
Present practical use cases for responsible implementation.

By closing the educational gap in AI fluency, this course will help urologists reclaim time, improve efficiency, reduce burnout, and lead the next wave of innovation in urologic care.

Learning Objective 1: Analyze the Basics of AI
By the end of this module, participants will possess a clear, intuitive grasp of the foundational principles that drive generative AI—how neural networks process and transform data, the role of training and fine-tuning in shaping model behavior, and the ways in which input prompts yield clinically meaningful outputs—while eschewing unnecessary mathematical complexity; furthermore, they will be equipped to approach AI-focused publications with a discerning eye, systematically dissecting study designs, data sources, validation methods, and potential biases, and will practice synthesizing evidence from multiple peer-reviewed articles to assess the rigor, reproducibility, and real-world applicability of AI innovations in urology.

Learning Objective 2: Use of AI in Clinical Urology
By the end of this session, participants will be able to recognize and articulate the key functionalities of cutting-edge AI tools designed to streamline and optimize urology clinic workflows—automating appointment triage, patient intake, and routine administrative tasks to free up clinician time—while understanding how generative models can autonomously conduct detailed clinical history taking and draft comprehensive outpatient visit notes; additionally, they will learn to deploy AI-driven diagnostic support systems that flag anomalies in imaging and laboratory data, thereby reducing cognitive overload, minimizing diagnostic errors, and ultimately enhancing patient safety and quality of care in their own practices.

Learning Objective 3: Use of AI in Urological Research
By the end of this segment, participants will be able to identify and leverage a spectrum of AI-enabled research platforms—from natural language processing tools that accelerate literature reviews and hypothesis generation to machine-learning algorithms that streamline data cleaning, statistical analysis, and visualizations—while rigorously adhering to established ethical frameworks and guidelines for responsible AI/ML and ChatGPT usage in scholarly work; moreover, they will explore cutting-edge applications of AI in surgical education and practice, including virtual reality–based simulation modules and intelligent robotic-surgery platforms that use real-time data to optimize procedural planning, intraoperative decision support, and post-operative debriefing, thereby enhancing both research productivity and clinical innovation.

title: 027IC - Case-Based Region-Based Urologic Management of Female Sexual Dysfunction
htmlDescription:
Course Description: This course will teach the urologist and advanced practice provider the skills needed to better communicate with patients with vulvas about their sexual health needs and better manage their sexual dysfunctions using contemporary region-based management strategies. This is especially important now that the AUA has developed practice guidelines for the management of genitourinary syndrome of menopause. The course will empower attendees to be “sex detectives.” After an initial overview of the 5 regions, diagnosis and treatment will be explained through various case studies, including an individual with hypoactive sexual desire disorder, with genitourinary syndrome of menopause, with anorgasmia, with dyspareunia, and with genito-pelvic dysesthesia. Normal physiology of function and pathophysiology of dysfunction will be described including how to examine the genitals under magnification to better understand sexual dysfunctions in people with vulvas. Diagnostic tools and treatment strategies for the management of desire, arousal, orgasm, and pain disorders including management of genitourinary syndrome of menopause issues will be discussed. Management strategies will move through the various regions (regions 1 – end organ, region 2 – pelvis/perineum, region 3 - cauda equina, region 4 - spinal cord, and region 5 – brain). Included in this course is an overview of how to use the latest FDA approved drugs including CNS drugs and, off label options, devices and surgical therapies. People with distressing sexual health concerns should undergo biopsychosocial diagnostic evaluations to assess pathophysiology, starting with a history and physical including vulvoscopy. How to perform a vulvoscopy and pelvic floor assessment will be demonstrated. Risks and benefits of hormone therapy for premenopausal women and women with genitourinary syndrome of menopause will be discussed. In addition, information about neurologic issues affecting sexual function will be presented. Also discussed are risk factors for female sexual dysfunction and co-morbid conditions such as genitourinary syndrome of menopause, interstitial cystitis/recurrent urinary tract infections and sexual dysfunction, clitoral phimosis and previous surgeries that can affect sexual function such as mid-urethral slings. People with vulvas presenting with urologic concerns may, in fact, have sexual dysfunction as their primary issue. This content is especially important for the urologist who treats sexual dysfunction in the male partner in a heterosexual couple, as the female partner may have concomitant sexual problems that need to be addressed.

Learning Objective 1: Associate basic science principles with physiology and pathophysiology of sexual function and dysfunction in individuals with vulvas

Learning Objective 2: Apply principles of history and physical examination to individuals with vulvas with sexual dysfunction

Learning Objective 3: Characterize region-based management of sexual problems in individuals with vulvas, as developed by the International Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health

Learning Objective 4: Employ principles of region-based management to diagnosis and treatment of genitourinary syndrome of menopause as elucidated by the AUA Guideline on GSM

Learning Objective 5: Diagnose and treat individuals with vulvas with various sexual dysfunctions presenting in a community setting with FDA-approved and off label medical therapies including estrogen (and progesterone) and androgen therapies as well as centrally-acting drugs

Learning Objective 6: Identify when sexual pain should be treated surgically

title: 028IC - Transition Urology - Lifelong Challenges and Complications

As these individuals age, they require not only ongoing medical and surgical management, but also psychosocial support to address the unique mental health challenges that often accompany their care journey.

This course will explore the reconstructive and surgical complexities encountered in adult patients with congenital anomalies and highlight the psychological sequelae of lifelong urological intervention—such as body image disturbance, treatment-related PTSD, anxiety around independence, and challenges to sexual function and fertility. A key focus will be the role of surgical planning within a comprehensive multidisciplinary framework, involving collaboration between pediatric and adult urologists, mental health professionals, physiatrists, and social support services.

Participants will gain insight into strategies for timing and selection of surgical interventions, managing previously operated anatomies, and addressing long-term functional outcomes. The course will emphasize patient-centered, trauma-informed care that integrates mental health about the complexitysupport into urological decision-making to optimize both surgical outcomes and patient quality of life.
The course aims to make transition urology a more accessible subject, with an introduction to service development and holistic care models.

title: 030IC - Urotrauma: Guidelines, Controversies, and Challenging Cases
htmlDescription:
Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive, case-based approach to the assessment and management of all types of urological injury, while focusing on trauma due to external violence (as opposed to iatrogenic injury). The course is highly relevant to both our domestic and international attendees, as we demonstrate diagnostic and treatment approaches that are relevant in both the technology-replete, as well as austere care environments. Given ongoing military conflicts abroad, we have expanded the discussion on military GU injuries, based on the large amount of data gathered during U.S. conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. Emphasis on the critical elements of related reconstructive surgery techniques are provided with case-based illustrations. Opportunities for audience participation are present throughout the course. The optimal working relationships between the urologist, the trauma surgeon, and other surgical and non-surgical specialists, are addressed. Specifically, learners will be able to take the following back to their respective practices after attending:
1. Obtain a full understanding of the most recent version of the AUA Urotrauma Guidelines.
2. Apply principles of damage control surgery to the management of unstable trauma patients with urological injuries.
3. Renal trauma: Understand the importance of nonoperative management of most renal injuries, reserving prompt intervention for those with high grade injury and ongoing hemorrhage and/or continued urinary extravasation.
4. Ureteral trauma: Maintain a high index of suspicion for ureteral trauma in high risk patients. Understand the importance of early intervention for ureteral injuries during the primary laparotomy when able. Consider endourologic or percutaneous approaches when ureteral injuries are diagnosed in a delayed manner.
5. Bladder trauma: Understand the importance of operative repair (intraperitoneal and complex extraperitoneal injuries) and nonoperative management (simple extraperitoneal injuries).
6. Urethral trauma: Diagnose and localize urethral injuries with retrograde urethrography. Appropriately manage urethral injuries based on injury mechanism and anatomical location.
7. Genital trauma: Stage and manage genital injuries with an appreciation for injury mechanism whether focal (i.e. penile fracture, penile amputation) or multi-system (i.e. blast trauma observed in military/combat settings). Understand the importance of long-term multidisciplinary care for genital injuries, given the potential for secondary interpersonal and mental health effects.

The course is divided into four sections, with the first three based on injury anatomy: Kidney/ureter, bladder/urethra, and external genitalia (male and female). These sections each begin with a didactic portion, focusing on injury evaluation and management (based on AUA guidelines) illustrated with numerous representative clinical cases. Each didactic portion is then augmented with an interactive portion, where attendees are invited to ask questions about their own complex and/or controversial clinical cases. In the fourth section, at least five interactive cases will be presented with clinical information and pictures/illustrations. The faculty will serve as a panel, addressing each of the cases. During this portion, the audience members are invited to the microphone to work through cases with the faculty panel and/or presenting difficult cases of their own. We believe that alternating between didactic and interactive formats throughout the course will lead to an energetic, engaging, and highly informative session.

Learning Objective 1: Describe guidelines-driven, evidence-based treatment algorithms for injuries to the kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra and external genitalia.

Learning Objective 2: Apply principles of damage control surgery to the management of unstable trauma patients with urological injuries.

Learning Objective 3: Distinguish between urological injuries that require non-operative surveillance, immediate surgery, and adjunctive interventions such as angio-embolization or endourologic management.

Learning Objective 4: Describe the unique challenges created by genitourinary injuries sustained in military/battlefield environments.

Learning Objective 5: Identify the importance of long-term multi-disciplinary care for the urinary, sexual, reproductive, interpersonal, and mental health sequelae which can result after urological injury.

title: 031IC - Male Chronic Pelvic Pain and Scrotal Pain: Common Clinical Scenarios, AUA Guidelines Review and Case-Based Discussion
htmlDescription:
Course Description: This course will focus on the AUA Guidelines and the current medical, surgical, pain management and multi-modal approaches to
the treatment of male pelvic pain. This will be presented in a case-based format with attention to the AUA Guidelines pertaining to these common etiologies. Surgical discussion (both microsurgical and robotic) will include the latest updates on microscopic denervation of the spermatic cord, cremasteric release, vasectomy reversal, epididymectomy, and varicocele repair. We will present the basic approach and the current
anatomical and pathological understanding of the disease process, as well as the most recent surgical
developments in the management of this common disorder. The role of appropriate preoperative
counseling, imaging, and evaluation, including the role of spermatic cord injection, will similarly be
reviewed. The course will provide evidence-based guidance and expert opinion on the preoperative
counseling and preparation, surgical technique, and postoperative considerations for surgical
treatments of chronic orchialgia and male pelvic pain. Practical tips on technique and intraoperative
decision making will also be discussed. As conservative therapy is generally the mainstay of treatment,
medical, physical therapy and pain management options will be comprehensively reviewed as well as
alternative and novel therapies to broaden the providers options when encountering these patients.
There will be a focus on the AUA guidelines and case management with time allotted for questions and discussion.

Learning Objective 1: Describe the key tenets of the evaluation of a male presenting with chronic pelvic pain and understand the benefits of an algorithmic and multidisciplinary approach.

Learning Objective 2: Recognize the pain management and physical therapy options to treat male pelvic pain and know when to refer.

Learning Objective 3: Determine when operative intervention may be appropriate in men with chronic pelvic pain and when nonoperative approaches are favored.

Learning Objective 4: Recognize the necessity of effective preoperative counseling in men considering surgical intervention for chronic pelvic pain.

title: 037IC - Evidence Behind the Needle: Trials, Technology, and Tradeoffs in Prostate Biopsy
htmlDescription:
Course Description: According to the AUA guidelines, post-biopsy infections can occur in 5-7% of patients, and hospitalization in 1-3% of patients. Hemorrhagic complications can require active intervention (procedure, hospitalization) in 2-3% of patients. Several reports indicate that post-biopsy infections following transrectal biopsy have been on the rise while others report a lower/stable risk of infections, ranging from < 1% to > 10%. The definition-dependent variability in reported risk of infection is also noted with transperineal biopsy, ranging from of 0.5% to 4% . Based on several observational studies of transperineal biopsy, a number of urologists have adopted the transperineal biopsy approach as the preferred alternative with the expectation of a near-zero risk of infections. Additionally, transperineal approach is thought to provide improved tissue sampling, with increased cancer detection rates. With that said, the high penetrance of transrectal biopsy (~80% in the US), would suggest that the transrectal approach is likely to remain a frequently utilized option.

Recently, several reports published within the last 18 months based on randomized clinical trials (RCTs) data comparing transrectal and transperineal biopsy provide much needed Level 1 evidence to inform our clinical practice. These RCTs demonstrate a disconnect between the expected outcomes and the actual outcomes, especially those related to diagnostic yield and complications, but also for patient-reported outcomes and health economics of the two biopsy procedures. Additional evidence from the ProBE-PC and TRANSLATE trials RCTs has been published on the diagnostic yield of the transrectal and transperineal biopsy. Equally important are the patient-reported outcomes from these trials which are now available. These reports demonstrate a significant differences between transrectal and transperineal biopsy related to patient experience (pain, urinary function) during and after prostate biopsy. Additionally, health economics data from these two trials are being analyzed which demonstrate the higher cost associated with transperineal approach. Thus, emerging evidence highlights the trade-offs regarding various clinically meaningful outcomes that are of interest to both the patients and the practitioners.

Although prostate cancer diagnosis represents a significant component of urologic practice, there has been a general lack of educational activities geared towards prostate biopsy procedures. Therefore, we are proposing an instructional course for the AUA 2026 annual conference for the target audience including practicing urologists, trainees, and APPs. The modifiable causes of complications will be outlined for each step of the procedure, followed by video-based discussion of measures to improve those outcomes. The course instructions will incorporate Level 1 evidence, and the lessons learned from RCTs to improve cancer diagnosis, reduce complications, and improve patient experience. Course participants will be able to incorporate data-driven changes to their prostate biopsy practice, appropriately select patients for the right biopsy procedure in light of the trade-offs and practice setting, identify modifiable causes of complications and implement procedural modifications to improve outcomes and patient experience.

Learning Objective 2: Appropriately select patients for the correct prostate biopsy procedure in light of relevant trade-offs between various outcomes.

Learning Objective 3: Identify modifiable steps of the procedure that are associated with infectious and non-infectious complications

Learning Objective 4: Incorporate procedural modifications to their biopsy technique to reduce the risk of complications and improve patient experience

Course Description: Robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy continues to evolve with the introduction and refinement of techniques aimed at improving functional and oncologic outcomes. This course provides a comprehensive overview of modern anatomic prostatectomy approaches, including pelvic fascia-sparing, Retzius-sparing, anterior pelvic fascia-sparing ("hood" technique), posterior nerve-sparing strategies, and single-port robotics. Participants will gain evidence-based insights into the surgical principles and technical execution of these methods.

Attendees will learn the anatomical rationale and technical nuances that underline these innovative approaches, supported by outcome data on urinary continence, sexual function, cancer control, and cost-effectiveness. The course will include didactic lectures from high-volume expert surgeons, detailed video demonstrations, and case-based discussions.

The course aims to empower practicing urologists, residents, and fellows with actionable knowledge and practical tips that can be applied across surgical settings. Emphasis will be placed on technique selection, troubleshooting challenging anatomy, managing complications, and balancing functional outcomes with oncologic safety.

Course Format
Traditional didactic lecture format supplemented with video demonstrations and case-based audience interaction. The two-hour course will consist of five 20-minute presentations delivered by expert faculty, followed by interactive Q&A. Each talk will focus on one of five key modern approaches:

Retzius-sparing prostatectomy
Anterior pelvic fascia-sparing "hood" technique
Posterior nerve-sparing and high anterior release
Single-port robotic prostatectomy
Pearls, pitfalls, and patient selection for functional and oncologic optimization

Attendees will leave with practical knowledge and technical confidence to implement or refine these techniques within their practice.

What is the problem we want to fix?
Urologists continue to seek better ways to preserve urinary and sexual function while achieving excellent oncologic control in radical prostatectomy. Adoption of advanced nerve-sparing and continence-preserving techniques remains inconsistent due to variability in training, a steep learning curve, and concerns regarding oncologic efficacy. As novel approaches like anterior pelvic fascia-sparing, posterior nerve-sparing, and single-port robotics emerge, there is a need for expert-led, evidence-based guidance on technique, outcomes, and case selection.

What is the reason for these gaps?
The field is advancing rapidly, yet formal training in newer techniques remains limited. Misconceptions persist regarding oncologic risk, and early concerns about positive surgical margins have contributed to hesitancy. Furthermore, comparative studies often vary in design or follow-up, making interpretation challenging. Our course addresses these educational needs by providing up-to-date literature review, technical walkthroughs, and expert opinion to increase surgeon competence, confidence, and outcome optimization.

This will lead into a discussion of prostate biopsy, including concepts crucial to reducing morbidity of prostate biopsy and improving patient experience. This course reviews available data regarding biopsy indications and techniques, including a strong emphasis on trans-perineal prostate biopsy. Additionally, this course fully explores the imperative of having a purposeful approach to biopsy aimed at diagnosing clinically significant disease while minimizing detection of clinically insignificant cancer. We also present the most current information regarding the use of image guided biopsy techniques, such as MRI-ultrasound fusion guided biopsy. Finally, we will look toward the future of prostate cancer diagnosis, including risk-stratified testing, combination of tests, sequencing of imaging and biomarkers and ongoing initiatives worldwide. Overall, the course provides an evidence-based and practical overview of methods to detect and diagnose clinically significant prostate cancer.

title: 053IC - Management of Complex Male Urinary Incontinence: Challenges and Strategies
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Urinary incontinence is estimated to be prevalent in about 14% of males in the United States. While the exact fraction among these patients suffering from stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is not definitively known, the major etiologies reported for SUI are prostatectomies with incontinence varying between 2% and 43% (depending on definition, surgical technique, and length of follow up), external beam radiation (1-16%), and transurethral resection of the prostate (1-3%). Besides pelvic floor physical therapy, established treatments of SUI are the implantation of either male slings or artificial urinary sphincters (AUS). While the majority of patients can be successfully treated with these options and the choice is mainly dependent on the degree of SUI, there are instances in which implantation of these devices is not straightforward and further considerations have to be considered. Examples of this include multiple prior AUS erosions, recurrent bladder neck contractures, concomitant radiation cystitis with recurrent hematuria, or decreased urethral viability due to prior radiation or urethroplasty. Also, and this is new for this application, for some patients, a urinary diversion is the best option, and we provide strategies to evaluate and select suitable patients.
There is limited information about each of these topics in the literature or textbooks, especially on how to successfully address SUI in these complex settings, and, hence, many patients may be left untreated despite viable therapeutic options. As the number of patients treated for prostate cancer has increased in the past 2-3 decades, so will the number of patients who present with complex SUI, making this an emergent and important topic for urologists.
While most SUI patients can be successfully treated with implantation of either a male sling or AUS, depending on the severity of incontinence or presence of prior radiation, there is a subset of patients when these procedures are at higher risk of complications. This is especially true for AUS placement. Many of these patients will not be offered an AUS or an AUS replacement after erosion or malfunction due to concerns of further complications. Similarly, patient co-morbidities such as recurrent hemorrhagic cystitis requiring repeated continuous bladder irrigations with large-bore catheters not compatible with an AUS or recurrent bladder neck contractures requiring interventions with cystoscopes of standard size may prevent urologists form implanting an AUS. There is also a subset of men in which AUS implantation, usually a second or third one, is simply not feasible due to lack of viable urethral tissue to support it. In all these instances, patients are left incontinent severely impacting their quality of life. Furthermore, the number of patients with complex incontinence will continue to increase, mainly as a result of late effects of prostate cancer therapy, specifically radiation and/or energy ablative treatments.

As the field of reconstructive surgery continues to emerge rapidly, so has the concern, understanding, and development of treatment options for patients with complex male incontinence. The educational aim of this course is to demonstrate the most common clinical presentations of these patients, to delineate treatment strategies, and to describe these treatment options.

Learning Objective 1: Recognize and to identify patients with complex male incontinence and to consider the challenges each patient faces and how to effectively and appropriately counsel him.

Learning Objective 2: Describe the challenges AUS placement can pose on patients with certain co-existing conditions such as hemorrhagic cystitis and recurrent bladder neck contracture and how AUS placement remains a feasible option.

Learning Objective 3: Recognize which patients are at increased risk for AUS erosions, how to mitigate these risks pre-operatively and to understand in which patients AUS placement or replacement remains an option.

Learning Objective 4: Identify patients that would be best addressed with urinary diversion.

title: 055IC - Prevention and Management of Complications in Robot-Assisted Surgery: Radical Prostatectomy, Radical Cystectomy and Partial Nephrectomy
htmlDescription:
Course Description: The course will be conducted by three distinguished surgeons, each with substantial and internationally recognized expertise in the field of robotic surgery. Drawing on their extensive clinical experience and academic background, the faculty will provide participants with a comprehensive educational program focused on the prevention and management of complications associated with major urologic robotic procedures.
The primary objective of the course is to deliver in-depth knowledge—both at a basic and advanced level—on intraoperative and postoperative complications encountered during robot-assisted radical prostatectomy, radical cystectomy, and partial nephrectomy. Emphasis will be placed not only on the identification and classification of such complications but also on evidence-based strategies to minimize their occurrence and optimize patient outcomes.
Through the use of interactive and case-based learning modules, participants will be exposed to real-world scenarios involving both frequent and less common adverse events. The course will offer practical guidance in the form of technical “tips and tricks” aimed at enhancing surgical safety and efficacy, as well as non-technical skills such as decision-making, teamwork, and crisis management. Furthermore, the curriculum will incorporate a detailed analysis of current international guidelines and recent literature, ensuring that learners are equipped with the most up-to-date and clinically relevant information. By the end of the course, participants will have acquired a structured approach to complication management in robotic urologic surgery, fostering improved surgical performance and patient care.

Learning Objective 1: Identify and assess complications commonly associated with robotic urologic surgical procedures. These include, but are not limited to, intraoperative bleeding, which may arise from vascular injury or inadequate hemostasis; rectal injuries, particularly in the context of radical prostatectomy, where proximity to the rectum increases the risk of unintentional damage; and urinary leakage, which can occur due to anastomotic failure or technical issues during ureteral or urethrovesical reconstruction. The course will emphasize the importance of early recognition through clinical signs, intraoperative indicators, and appropriate imaging modalities, as well as the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying each complication. Particular attention will be given to risk stratification, predictive factors, and intraoperative decision-making strategies aimed at minimizing harm and improving patient outcomes.

Learning Objective 2: Implement evidence-based strategies and operative techniques aimed at minimizing the risk of intraoperative and postoperative complications. A central focus will be placed on preventive actions that can be integrated into the perioperative workflow to enhance patient safety and surgical outcomes. Key areas of emphasis will include the appropriate identification and selection of candidates for lymph node dissection (LND), ensuring that the indication is based on robust oncologic criteria in order to avoid unnecessary morbidity associated with extended dissections. Moreover, the course will address the importance of correct patient positioning, with particular reference to the prevention of position-related peripheral neuropathies, such as femoral or brachial plexus injuries, which can occur due to prolonged operative times or suboptimal padding and alignment. Participants will also explore the role of preoperative patient optimization and selection, including the evaluation of comorbidities, body habitus, and prior surgical history, in reducing the likelihood of avoidable intra- and postoperative complications. The course will encourage a multidisciplinary approach, incorporating anesthesia, nursing, and postoperative care perspectives to develop a comprehensive and anticipatory strategy for complication prevention.

Learning Objective 3: Effectively manage both intraoperative and postoperative complications, through a combination of theoretical instruction and case-based discussion. The Faculty will present evidence-based recommendations and guideline-approved strategies for addressing a broad spectrum of clinical scenarios, ranging from common to rare but potentially severe complications. Particular attention will be devoted to the systematic approach to complication management, including early recognition, diagnostic workup, decision-making algorithms, and appropriate therapeutic interventions. Among the complications to be covered are recto-vesical fistulas, a rare but serious event often requiring complex surgical repair and multidisciplinary coordination; postoperative lymphoceles, which may necessitate percutaneous drainage, sclerotherapy, or surgical intervention depending on their size, location, and symptomatology; and management of lymphedema, especially in patients undergoing extended pelvic lymph node dissection, with discussion of both conservative and interventional approaches. Real-world cases and video-based demonstrations will support the development of both technical and non-technical competencies, including crisis resource management, communication with the operative team, and informed dialogue with patients regarding complication-related outcomes.

We will discuss importance considerations both preoperatively and postoperatively to set practitioners up for success to help these men navigate the quality-of-life concerns such as sperm cryopreservation, oncoTESE, management of hypogonadism postoperatively, etc. The approach to these decisions and important clinical considerations will be discussed using guideline-based considerations and situations that go beyond the guidelines. This course will allow participants to better understand the comprehensive management of the entire testicular cancer patient from cancer treatment to quality-of-life concerns related to the cancer treatments.

Learning Objective 1: Describe the imaging, laboratory, and treatment workup of patient with early-stage testicular cancer

Learning Objective 2: Define surgical decision-making for testicular cancer patients in the post-chemotherapy setting

Learning Objective 3: Describe the surgical and medical management of infertility concerns and hypogonadal state in men with testicular cancer

title: 064IC - Conquering the Learning Curve of Single Port Robotic Surgery : A Step by Step Approach Using Video Based Instruction
htmlDescription:
Course Description: The initial SP adoption period represents a discovery phase, during which a restricted number of experienced surgeons have attempted to make the most of this new technology. This was particularly important in adaptation from the da Vinci Xi to the SP robot, as although the new features of the SP platform allow novel strategies, they have added complexity to procedures. .
Most urologists approaching Single Port surgery focus on technical aspects of the single port robot and neglect the modifications required in the surgical approach to adopt the novel platform. Urologists whom have sucessfully adopted SP surgery , advance through the learning curve of SP surgery by progressively adopting their approach and overcomming the technical challanges . In this course proposal, we aim to implement educational interventions to address skills for practicing urologists wishing to adopt Single Port robotic approach.
In this course proposal, we aim to implement a video-based step by step educational strategies to address technical barriers for practicing urologists wishing to adopt Single Port robotic approach. We intend to achieve this by presenting unique perspective from 3 urologist who meticulously modified their conventional robotic approach to suit that of Single Port surgery eventually transforming their practice to Single Port robotics. Although the single-incision approach, offers potential benefits it also presents unique challenges for the surgical assistant in comparison to the multiport approach. In response, a Physician Assistant specializing in robotic bedside assistance was added to the faculty to address this gap.

This course serves to develop knowledge, skills and attitudes that most urologist are unfamiliar with but are rapidly becoming a part of patient care in today’s healthcare landscape. This course will be led by a group of directors and faculty who have a significant experience with the SP platform. Each Faculty will focus on a specific robotic procedure (Radical Prostatectomy, Partial Nephrectomy, Trans vesical prostate enucleation), each describing the evolution and modification to their approach, technical aspects, patient selection, and most importantly how to overcome complications. in addition, a PA specializing in robotic bed side assistance will guide the particpants (Urologists and other APPs) on specifics to the single-port platform.
This course differs from other similar courses in that it will focus on how a surgeon can modify their procedure in a stepwise manner to safely adopt this novel technology without compromising patient care. All presentations will focus on video-based step by step instruction for the 3 surgical procedures, offering side by side comparisons of single port vs multiport for cirtical steps of the 3 procedures.

To optimize the particpants understanding of the material several educational pedagogy will be utilized:
1- Audience particpation and reflection through polls embedded into the faculty presentations
2- Presentations will focus on video based step by step instructions of cases (similar to semi-live surgeries)
3- Q&A sessions inbetween each presentation to encourge interactive discussions with the audience

Learning Objective 1: 1) Acquire the Knowledge required to safety adopt the single port robotic platform.
a. Understand the hardware/software differences between multiport and single port robotic platforms including the benefits and limitations of each technology.
b. Understand and explain the approaches, access , procedure modifications, post operative course unique to single port robotic surgery.

Learning Objective 2: 2) Apply all the knowledge and approaches required to perform complex procedures (namely ; Extraperitoenal Radical Prostatectomy, Retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy and transvesical enucleation of the prostate) safety using the single port robotic platform .
a. Understand the unique access/docking methods and approaches for SP robot
b. Understand the various applications of the flexible SP camera
c. Understand the various applications of the SP instruments
d. Understand with various orientation of SP instruments and camera to complete a series of critical steps for the 3 procedures
e. Tips and trick to to successfully and safely adopt the procedure
c. Understand how to avoid and manage complications that may arise from performing SP robotic surgery

Learning Objective 3: 3) Understand how to utilize the bed side assistant during these procedures including.
a. Port Placement: Accurately placing the ports under direct vision to ensure optimal space and prevent injury to vital structures.
b. Instrument Handling: Familiarity with laparoscopic instruments and their use in single-port surgery.
c. Traction and Retraction: Providing adequate traction and retraction to aid in tissue dissection.
d. Suction and Irrigation: Performing suctioning and irrigating to maintain a clear surgical field.
e. Safety Monitoring: Ensuring patient safety by monitoring the patient's position, robotic arms to prevent injury and particular issues related to insufflation.
Overall, the bedside assistant plays a vital role in single-port robotic surgery, contributing to the success of the procedure by providing essential support and ensuring patient safety within the constraints of the single-port approach.

title: 065IC - Optimizing Clinical Workflow in Urology: Leveraging KPIs and AI
htmlDescription:
Course Description: Are you a urologist, advanced practice provider or clinical administrator seeking to improve workflow, increase revenue and enhance patient outcomes? This specialized workshop is designed for professionals in urology who want to lead impactful changes in clinical operations through strategic use of key performance indicators and artificial intelligence. Participants will learn how to identify, measure, and act upon KPIs specific to urology practices. The course will demonstrate how AI can be used to improve revenue cycle management, streamline patient interactions, and support clinical decision-making, including areas such as coding, billing, prior authorizations, and cancer surveillance. While AI holds immense potential, its integration poses challenges, including cultural resistance, data quality concerns, and regulatory hurdles. Attendees will explore real-world strategies for overcoming these barriers—building trust in AI tools, mitigating bias, and training teams effectively—while maintaining a strong commitment to patient-centered care. Through case-based examples and interactive discussion, attendees will leave with actionable tools and a roadmap for optimizing their practice’s efficiency and outcomes.

Learning Objective 1: Identify and apply KPIs relevant to clinical workflow, patient access, and financial health in urology practices.

Learning Objective 2: Evaluate opportunities for AI integration in front-desk operations, clinical decision-making, coding/billing, prior authorizations, and cancer follow-up.

Learning Objective 3: Analyze the challenges of AI implementation, including data quality, bias, regulatory constraints, and cultural resistance within clinical teams.

Learning Objective 4: Develop practical strategies to train staff and build trust in AI-driven tools while maintaining patient-centered care.

Learning Objective 5: Design and lead a practice improvement initiative using KPIs and AI to enhance clinical management, patient experience, and operational efficiency.
